hook.en: You decide to buy 10 shares. Within a day they appear in your account, with no paper at all. Here is what happens in between.

objectives.en: Outline the trading procedure on a stock exchange
Explain dematerialisation and the role of depositories
Describe settlement on the T+1 cycle

narration.en: You decide to buy 10 shares. Within a day they appear in your account, with no paper at all. Here is what happens in between.

body.en: Steps: select a SEBI-registered broker (stockbroker); open a trading account with the broker and a demat account with a depository participant (DP), completing KYC with PAN and bank details; place an order (buy or sell, quantity, market order or limit price) online or through the broker; the order is matched electronically on the exchange's screen-based system and executed; the broker issues a contract note giving the details of the trade; and the trade is settled: money is paid and shares are delivered through the clearing corporation.

title.en: On the board: demat and depositories

say.en: Dematerialisation: converting paper share certificates into electronic form held in a demat account.

text.en: Depositories in India: NSDL and CDSL
Depository participants (DPs): banks and brokers who
serve investors on behalf of the depositories
No risk of loss, theft, forgery or damage of paper
Quick transfer; no stamp duty on transfer of demat shares
India moved to the T+1 cycle (completed in 2023):
money and shares settle one working day after the trade

steps.en: Open a trading account and a demat account with KYC

The broker sends a contract note
On T+1 the money is paid and shares are credited to the demat account

explanation.en: From choosing a broker to settlement on the next working day.

body.en: A market order buys or sells at the best available price at once; a limit order is executed only at the price set or better; a stop-loss order sells automatically if the price falls to a set level, limiting the loss. Every trade carries charges: brokerage, securities transaction tax (STT), exchange transaction charges, SEBI fees, stamp duty and GST on services. The investor's gain on a trade is the change in price times the quantity, minus these charges, plus any dividend received.
